claim: Trace conditioning and extinction learning depend on the hippocampus.
source: Trace conditioning and extinction learning depend on the hippocampus, but it remains unclear how neural activity in the hippocampus is modulated during these two different behavioral processes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact that motivates the study.

claim: Distinct populations of CA1 cells contribute to trace conditioned learning versus extinction learning.
source: Our findings reveal that distinct populations of CA1 cells contribute to trace conditioned learning versus extinction learning, as learning emerges.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: CA1 network connectivity patterns differ between conditioning and extinction.
source: Furthermore, we examined network connectivity by calculating co-activity between CA1 neuron pairs and found that CA1 network connectivity patterns also differ between conditioning and extinction, even though the overall connectivity density remains constant.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by co-occurrence matrix analysis in the results.

claim: Overall connectivity density remains constant between conditioning and extinction.
source: Furthermore, we examined network connectivity by calculating co-activity between CA1 neuron pairs and found that CA1 network connectivity patterns also differ between conditioning and extinction, even though the overall connectivity density remains constant.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Distinct populations of hippocampal CA1 neurons form different sub-networks with unique connectivity patterns that encode different aspects of learning.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that distinct populations of hippocampal CA1 neurons, forming different sub-networks with unique connectivity patterns, encode different aspects of learning.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, synthesizing the findings about distinct cell populations and network patterns.

claim: Early surgical lesions of the hippocampus in human patients resulted in severe memory loss and an inability to form new declarative or episodic memories.
source: Early surgical lesions of the hippocampus in human patients, designed to alleviate intractable epilepsy, resulted in severe memory loss and an inability to form new declarative or episodic memories (Scoville and Milner, 1957; Scoville, 1954).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Scoville and Milner, 1957 and Scoville, 1954.

claim: Hippocampal atrophy is associated with diseases related to memory loss and cognitive decline, including dementia and Alzheimer's disease.
source: Hippocampal atrophy is also associated with diseases related to memory loss and cognitive decline, including dementia and Alzheimer's disease (Fein et al., 2000; Apostolova et al., 2010; Chow et al., 2012; Henneman et al., 2009; Camicioli et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The hippocampus is important for spatial, contextual, and associative learning in a variety of animal models.
source: Many mechanistic studies have highlighted the importance of the hippocampus for spatial, contextual, and associative learning in a variety of animal models (Wirth et al., 2009; Jarrard, 1993).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wirth et al., 2009 and Jarrard, 1993.

claim: Trace eye-blink conditioning requires an intact hippocampus.
source: One such well-established paradigm is trace eye-blink conditioning, which requires an intact hippocampus (McEchron et al., 1998; Moyer et al., 2015; Tseng et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McEchron et al., 1998; Moyer et al., 2015; Tseng et al., 2004.

claim: In trace conditioning, the CS and US are separated temporally by a quiescent memory trace interval.
source: In trace conditioning, the CS and US are separated temporally by a quiescent memory trace interval.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about trace conditioning paradigm.

claim: Over time, subjects learn to associate the CS with the US, generating a behavioral conditioned response to the CS.
source: Over time, subjects learn to associate the CS with the US, generating a behavioral conditioned response to the CS (Gruart and Delgado-García, 2007; Li et al., 2008; McLaughlin et al., 2002; Kishimoto et al., 2001; Kronforst-Collins and Disterhoft, 1998; Takehara-Nishiuchi and McNaughton, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing trace conditioning behavior.

claim: Trace conditioning acquisition is thought to depend on signaling at both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors.
source: Trace conditioning acquisition is thought to depend on signaling at both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors (Brown et al., 2010; Disterhoft et al., 1999; Fontán-Lozano et al., 2005; Raybuck and Gould, 2010; Woodruff-Pak, 2003; Woodruff-Pak et al., 2007; Flesher et al., 2011; Woodruff-Pak et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Trace conditioning involves NMDA receptor-dependent plasticity.
source: and involves NMDA receptor-dependent plasticity (Sakamoto et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sakamoto et al., 2005.

claim: The hippocampus is required for context-dependent extinction learning.
source: The hippocampus is also required for context-dependent extinction learning (Moyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moyer et al., 2015.

claim: Extinction learning is traditionally considered new learning that overrides a previously learned relationship.
source: Traditionally, extinction learning is considered new learning that overrides a previously learned relationship.
evidence: This is a statement about the traditional understanding of extinction learning.

claim: Extinction learning has been shown to be NMDA receptor-dependent.
source: Extinction learning has also been shown to be NMDA receptor-dependent (Dillon et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Dillon et al., 2008.

claim: Extinction learning requires the involvement of hippocampal inhibitory neurons.
source: and requires the involvement of hippocampal inhibitory neurons (Lissek et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lissek et al., 2017.

claim: Extinction learning requires adult neurogenesis.
source: and adult neurogenesis (Catlow et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Catlow et al., 2013.

claim: In both the CA1 and dentate gyrus distinct populations of neurons were activated in fear conditioning and context-dependent fear extinction.
source: Immediate early gene and synaptic tagging experiments revealed that in both the CA1 and dentate gyrus distinct populations of neurons were activated in fear conditioning and context-dependent fear extinction (Tronson et al., 2009; Lacagnina et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tronson et al., 2009 and Lacagnina et al., 2019.

claim: Zhang et al. identified a population of CA1 neurons that emerges to encode contextual fear conditioning using calcium imaging.
source: To address this question, Zhang et al. recently identified a population of CA1 neurons that emerges to encode contextual fear conditioning using calcium imaging, but they did not examine whether different neuron populations were actively recruited during extinction training (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Zhang et al. did not examine whether different neuron populations were actively recruited during extinction training.
source: To address this question, Zhang et al. recently identified a population of CA1 neurons that emerges to encode contextual fear conditioning using calcium imaging, but they did not examine whether different neuron populations were actively recruited during extinction training (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the Zhang et al. study.

claim: Calcium imaging allows measurement of several hundreds of neurons simultaneously with single-cell resolution across many trials.
source: Calcium imaging allows us to measure several hundreds of neurons simultaneously with single-cell resolution across many trials, and in the same brain area over multiple days of learning (Mohammed et al., 2016; Hansen et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2016 and Hansen et al., 2018.

claim: Hippocampal-dependent trace conditioning is well-suited to calcium imaging because generally both learning and the associated CA1 neuronal responses evolve gradually.
source: Hippocampal-dependent trace conditioning is well-suited to calcium imaging because generally both learning and the associated CA1 neuronal responses evolve gradually, unlike fear conditioning, in which learning can occur as rapidly as a single trial.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement explaining why trace conditioning was chosen for this study.

claim: Different individual CA1 neurons showed CS-related responses during either trace conditioning or extinction learning.
source: Our results indicate that different individual CA1 neurons showed CS-related responses during either trace conditioning or extinction learning, suggesting two functionally distinct sub-populations of cells within hippocampal CA1.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section.

claim: Distinct pairs of neurons are activated during trace conditioning versus extinction learning.
source: We found that distinct pairs of neurons are activated during trace conditioning versus extinction learning, highlighting differential network activity during these two learning processes.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the results section.

claim: Conditioned responding increases across trace conditioning sessions in a classical eye-blink task.
source: Conditioned responding increases across trace conditioning sessions in a classical eye-blink task and decreases during extinction learning
evidence: This is a section heading and is supported by behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: Conditioned responding decreases during extinction learning.
source: Conditioned responding increases across trace conditioning sessions in a classical eye-blink task and decreases during extinction learning
evidence: This is a section heading and is supported by behavioral data in Figure 2.

claim: Trace conditioning experiments were performed in head-fixed mice (n = 9 mice).
source: Trace conditioning experiments were performed in head-fixed mice (n = 9 mice) that were positioned under a custom wide-field microscope equipped with a scientific (sCMOS) camera, as previously described (Mohammed et al., 2016; Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup and sample size.

claim: Calcium activity in CA1 neurons was monitored via GCaMP6f fluorescence.
source: Calcium activity in CA1 neurons was monitored via GCaMP6f fluorescence, which allows recording from hundreds of neurons simultaneously (Mohammed et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2013; Gritton et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the imaging method used in the study.

claim: GCaMP6f fluorescence allows recording from hundreds of neurons simultaneously.
source: Calcium activity in CA1 neurons was monitored via GCaMP6f fluorescence, which allows recording from hundreds of neurons simultaneously (Mohammed et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2013; Gritton et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2013; Gritton et al., 2019.

claim: Mice were injected with AAV-Synapsin-GCaMP6f prior to imaging.
source: Prior to imaging, mice were injected with AAV-Synapsin-GCaMP6f and implanted with a custom window that allowed optical access to dorsal CA1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the viral injection procedure.

claim: Mice were implanted with a custom window that allowed optical access to dorsal CA1.
source: Prior to imaging, mice were injected with AAV-Synapsin-GCaMP6f and implanted with a custom window that allowed optical access to dorsal CA1 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for imaging access.

claim: 4–6 weeks after surgery, mice were habituated and trained on a classical trace eye-blink conditioning paradigm followed by an extinction training session.
source: 4–6 weeks after surgery, mice were habituated and trained on a classical trace eye-blink conditioning paradigm followed by an extinction training session (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental timeline.

claim: The conditioning paradigm consisted of a 9500 Hz, 350 ms tone as a CS, followed by a 250 ms trace interval, which was then followed by a 100 ms gentle puff of air to one eye that served as the US.
source: The conditioning paradigm consisted of a 9500 Hz, 350 ms tone as a CS, followed by a 250 ms trace interval, which was then followed by a 100 ms gentle puff of air to one eye that served as the US (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the specific parameters of the trace conditioning paradigm.

claim: Animals were trained for 60–80 CS-US trials over 5–9 days until they reached conditioned response criterion (anticipatory eyelid movement on 65% of trials).
source: Animals were trained for 60–80 CS-US trials over 5–9 days until they reached conditioned response criterion (anticipatory eyelid movement on 65% of trials, described below).
evidence: This describes the training protocol and criterion for learning.

claim: After reliable conditioned response to CS presentations was established, on the final day of imaging, animals were given a block of 20–40 CS-US trials, followed by a block of 40 CS-only trials.
source: After reliable conditioned response to CS presentations was established, on the final day of imaging, animals were given a block of 20–40 CS-US trials, followed by a block of 40 CS-only trials, where the CS was not followed by the US (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for the final imaging session.

claim: The final 20 conditioning trials were analyzed in the first imaging day (first training session) and the last imaging day (last training session).
source: To compare across different learning conditions, the final 20 conditioning trials were analyzed in the first imaging day (first training session) and the last imaging day (last training session).
evidence: This describes the analysis approach for comparing learning conditions.

claim: Both the first 20 and final 20 CS-only extinction trials were analyzed (extinction session trials 1–20 and trials 21–40, respectively).
source: Because extinction learning emerges over time, we analyzed both the first 20 and final 20 CS-only extinction trials (extinction session trials 1–20 and trials 21–40, respectively) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the analysis approach for extinction trials.

claim: Spontaneous eye closures occurred in about 20% of the 600 ms windows analyzed during the non-stimulus periods and remained stable across sessions.
source: We first estimated basal spontaneous eye closure occurrence by examining the 'non-stimulus periods' of each trial, defined as the time periods that are more than 2 s before a tone onset or more than 8 s after a tone onset. Spontaneous eye closures occurred in about 20% of the 600 ms windows analyzed during the non-stimulus periods and remained stable across sessions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about baseline eye closure behavior.

claim: For all animals, conditioned eye closure occurrence during the first session was significantly higher than the spontaneous eye closure occurrence (p=0.0003, n = 9 mice, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
source: For all animals, conditioned eye closure occurrence during the first session was significantly higher than the spontaneous eye closure occurrence (p=0.0003, n = 9 mice, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing conditioned and spontaneous eye closures.

claim: Most animals (n = 7 mice) showed gradual learning acquisition over the first training session with an eye closure occurrence of 30–70% during the tone-puff window.
source: While most animals (n = 7 mice) showed gradual learning acquisition over the first training session with an eye closure occurrence of 30–70% during the tone-puff window, two animals exhibited rapid learning and correctly responded to over 75% of first session trials.
evidence: This describes the behavioral learning patterns observed in the animals.

claim: Two animals exhibited rapid learning and correctly responded to over 75% of first session trials.
source: While most animals (n = 7 mice) showed gradual learning acquisition over the first training session with an eye closure occurrence of 30–70% during the tone-puff window, two animals exhibited rapid learning and correctly responded to over 75% of first session trials.
evidence: This describes the behavioral learning patterns observed in a subset of animals.

claim: After reaching conditioned response criterion over several days of training, all animals maintained a conditioned response occurrence of 55–90% during the last training session.
source: After reaching conditioned response criterion over several days of training, all animals maintained a conditioned response occurrence of 55–90% during the last training session, again significantly higher than the spontaneous eye closure occurrence (p=0.0003, n = 9 mice, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This describes the behavioral performance after training.

claim: The two rapid learners that achieved over 75% conditioned responding during the first session were excluded from analysis involving comparisons between the first and last training sessions.
source: In order to examine how CA1 neural activity changes during learning, we verified conditioned learning by comparing behavioral responses between the first and last days of training. To most accurately capture the effects of learning that occurs after many days of training, we excluded the two rapid learners that achieved over 75% conditioned responding during the first session from analysis involving comparisons between the first and last training sessions.
evidence: This describes an exclusion criterion for certain analyses.

claim: The remaining seven animals showed significantly more conditioned responding during the last training session (68.9 ± 11.9%) compared to the first training session (45.0 ± 16.8%, p=0.025, n = 7 mice, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
source: The remaining seven animals showed significantly more conditioned responding during the last training session (68.9 ± 11.9%) compared to the first training session (45.0 ± 16.8%, p=0.025, n = 7 mice, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 2A, Bi).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing learning improvement over training.

claim: Conditioned responding trended downward throughout the extinction session.
source: Next, we analyzed performance during the extinction session and found that conditioned responding trended downward throughout the extinction session (Figure 2Bii).
evidence: This describes the behavioral trend during extinction.

claim: By the end of the extinction session, most animals exhibited significantly reduced conditioned responding compared to the last training session.
source: By the end of the extinction session, most animals exhibited significantly reduced conditioned responding compared to the last training session.
evidence: This describes the behavioral outcome of extinction training.

claim: Across all animals, the conditioned response dropped to 47.8 ± 21.1% during trials 21–40 of the extinction session, significantly lower than the conditioned response rate during the last training session (p=0.034, n = 9 mice, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
source: Across all animals, the conditioned response dropped to 47.8 ± 21.1% during trials 21–40 of the extinction session, significantly lower than the conditioned response rate during the last training session (p=0.034, n = 9 mice, Wilcoxon rank-sum test, Figure 2A, Bii).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing extinction learning.

claim: 3241 and 2332 total neurons were recorded in the first and last/extinction sessions respectively.
source: To evaluate how CA1 neural activity is modulated between the first and last sessions of conditioning training, we imaged a large number of individual CA1 neurons during trace conditioning (3241 and 2332 total neurons recorded in the first and last/extinction sessions respectively, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This provides the sample size of neurons recorded.

claim: The basal calcium event rate was 1.7 ± 0.4 events/min (0.03 ± 0.006 events/s) during the non-stimulus periods (n = 297,336 events, across n = 9 animals from n = 27 sessions).
source: Consistent with previous observations of sparse calcium events (Gritton et al., 2019), we found that the basal calcium event rate was 1.7 ± 0.4 events/min (0.03 ± 0.006 events/s) during the non-stimulus periods (n = 297,336 events, across n = 9 animals from n = 27 sessions).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about baseline calcium activity.

claim: After multiple days of conditioning, 14.7% of neurons met the criteria as responsive to the tone during the last training session (286 responsive neurons of total 1946 recorded neurons in seven mice).
source: After multiple days of conditioning, 14.7% of neurons met the criteria as responsive to the tone during the last training session (286 responsive neurons of total 1946 recorded neurons in seven mice, Supplementary file 2), significantly greater than the responsive population during the first training session (12.2%, 288 responsive neurons of total 2367 recorded neurons from seven mice, p=0.017, Fisher's exact test, Figure 2Ci, Di, Ei, Supplementary file 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about responsive neurons after conditioning.

claim: The responsive population during the last training session was significantly greater than the responsive population during the first training session (p=0.017, Fisher's exact test).
source: After multiple days of conditioning, 14.7% of neurons met the criteria as responsive to the tone during the last training session (286 responsive neurons of total 1946 recorded neurons in seven mice, Supplementary file 2), significantly greater than the responsive population during the first training session (12.2%, 288 responsive neurons of total 2367 recorded neurons from seven mice, p=0.017, Fisher's exact test, Figure 2Ci, Di, Ei, Supplementary file 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing responsive neurons between sessions.

claim: Calcium response latency was significantly shorter during the last training session (337.6 ± 202.5 ms) as compared to the first training session (436.9 ± 202.9 ms, p=0.001, one-way ANOVA post-hoc Tukey test, n = 795 neurons).
source: In addition to the increase in the fraction of responsive cells after conditioning training, calcium response latency was significantly shorter during the last training session (337.6 ± 202.5 ms) as compared to the first training session (436.9 ± 202.9 ms, p=0.001, one-way ANOVA post-hoc Tukey test, n = 795 neurons, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about response timing changes with training.

claim: Shorter calcium response latency indicates that with repeated training CA1 neurons shift their responsivity closer to the CS tone presentations.
source: Shorter calcium response latency indicates that with repeated training CA1 neurons shift their responsivity closer to the CS tone presentations, further confirming more robust CA1 responses after trace conditioning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the latency data.

claim: CA1 neurons begin to encode the CS on the first day of training, and they more reliably encode the CS over several days of continued conditioning training.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Zhang et al., 2019), our findings demonstrate that CA1 neurons begin to encode the CS on the first day of training, and they more reliably encode the CS over several days of continued conditioning training.
evidence: This is a summary statement of findings, consistent with prior work.

claim: 11.4% of neurons were responsive to the tone during the first 20 trials of the extinction session (266 responsive neurons from total 2332 recorded cells in nine mice).
source: We found that 11.4% of neurons were responsive to the tone during the first 20 trials of the extinction session (266 responsive neurons from total 2332 recorded cells in nine mice, Supplementary file 3), significantly less than the 14.9% responsive neurons during the last training session and similar to the 12.2% responsive neurons during the first session (p=0.0005, n = 9 mice for last session vs. extinction session and p=0.92, n = 7 mice for first session vs. extinction session, Fisher's exact test, Figure 2Ei, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about responsive neurons during extinction.

claim: The percentage of responsive neurons during the extinction session was significantly less than the 14.9% responsive neurons during the last training session (p=0.0005, n = 9 mice, Fisher's exact test).
source: We found that 11.4% of neurons were responsive to the tone during the first 20 trials of the extinction session (266 responsive neurons from total 2332 recorded cells in nine mice, Supplementary file 3), significantly less than the 14.9% responsive neurons during the last training session and similar to the 12.2% responsive neurons during the first session (p=0.0005, n = 9 mice for last session vs. extinction session and p=0.92, n = 7 mice for first session vs. extinction session, Fisher's exact test, Figure 2Ei, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing responsive neurons between last training and extinction sessions.

claim: The percentage of responsive neurons during the extinction session was similar to the 12.2% responsive neurons during the first session (p=0.92, n = 7 mice, Fisher's exact test).
source: We found that 11.4% of neurons were responsive to the tone during the first 20 trials of the extinction session (266 responsive neurons from total 2332 recorded cells in nine mice, Supplementary file 3), significantly less than the 14.9% responsive neurons during the last training session and similar to the 12.2% responsive neurons during the first session (p=0.0005, n = 9 mice for last session vs. extinction session and p=0.92, n = 7 mice for first session vs. extinction session, Fisher's exact test, Figure 2Ei, Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding comparing responsive neurons between first and extinction sessions.

claim: The reduction in responsive neurons during the extinction session is likely a reflection of the network remodeling that is occurring during extinction learning.
source: The reduction in responsive neurons during the extinction session is likely a reflection of the network remodeling that is occurring during extinction learning, which would not have been present in the late training session as conditioned learning was well-established during that session.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the reduction in responsive neurons.

claim: The existence of a responsive population during the extinction session demonstrates that neurons in CA1 show new encoding of the CS during extinction learning, after it is no longer paired with the US.
source: However, the existence of this responsive population during the extinction session demonstrates that neurons in CA1 show new encoding of the CS during extinction learning, after it is no longer paired with the US.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the presence of responsive neurons during extinction.

claim: The Jaccard index for the common responsive cells between the two trial blocks of the late training session was 20.5%.
source: The Jaccard index for the common responsive cells between the two trial blocks of the late training session was 20.5%, significantly greater than the Jaccard index observed between the last training and extinction sessions (10.7%, p=1.88e-6, n = 9 mice, Fisher's exact test, Figure 2Eii, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about cell overlap within a training session.

claim: The Jaccard index for common responsive cells between the last training and extinction sessions was 10.7%, significantly less than the Jaccard index between the two trial blocks of the late training session (p=1.88e-6, n = 9 mice, Fisher's exact test).
source: The Jaccard index for the common responsive cells between the two trial blocks of the late training session was 20.5%, significantly greater than the Jaccard index observed between the last training and extinction sessions (10.7%, p=1.88e-6, n = 9 mice, Fisher's exact test, Figure 2Eii, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing distinct cell populations between conditioning and extinction.

claim: During extinction learning, in less than 20 trials, a largely unique population of neurons is recruited to encode tone presentations.
source: Together, these results suggest that during extinction learning, in less than 20 trials, a largely unique population of neurons is recruited to encode tone presentations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Jaccard index analysis.

claim: CO cells exhibited calcium events on 13.3 ± 2.3% of trials during the last training session.
source: CO cells exhibited calcium events on 13.3 ± 2.3% of trials during the last training session, and EX cells exhibited calcium events on 7.0 ± 1.0% of trials during the extinction session.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the sparseness of CO cell responses.

claim: EX cells exhibited calcium events on 7.0 ± 1.0% of trials during the extinction session.
source: CO cells exhibited calcium events on 13.3 ± 2.3% of trials during the last training session, and EX cells exhibited calcium events on 7.0 ± 1.0% of trials during the extinction session.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the sparseness of EX cell responses.

claim: Most neurons individually contributed to encoding only a small fraction of trials.
source: Because most neurons individually contributed to encoding only a small fraction of trials, trial encoding may thus depend on the contributions of a large population of sparsely active neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the sparse response data.

claim: Trial encoding may depend on the contributions of a large population of sparsely active neurons.
source: Because most neurons individually contributed to encoding only a small fraction of trials, trial encoding may thus depend on the contributions of a large population of sparsely active neurons.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the sparse response data.

claim: Both CO and EX cells are not significantly clustered near one another and are heterogeneously distributed throughout the hippocampus.
source: Comparing the spatial distributions of cells indicates that both CO and EX cells are not significantly clustered near one another and are heterogeneously distributed throughout the hippocampus (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This is a finding about spatial organization supported by spatial analysis and Figure 3C, D.

claim: 3.8 ± 2.9% of cells within a 100 µm radius of CO cells were other CO cells, which was not significantly different from that expected by random shuffling of cell identity (shuffled = 2.8%, N = 1000, p=0.17, two-tailed bootstrap, α = 0.05).
source: We found that 3.8 ± 2.9% of cells within a 100 µm radius of CO cells were other CO cells, which was not significantly different from that expected by random shuffling of cell identity (shuffled = 2.8%, N = 1000, p=0.17, two-tailed bootstrap, α = 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about spatial clustering of CO cells.

claim: 2.3 ± 2.6% of cells within a 100 µm radius of EX cells were other EX cells, which was not significantly different from that expected by random shuffling (shuffled = 1.8%, N = 1000, p=0.24, two-tailed bootstrap, α = 0.05).
source: Similarly, 2.3 ± 2.6% of cells within a 100 µm radius of EX cells were other EX cells, which was also not significantly different from that expected by random shuffling (shuffled = 1.8%, N = 1000, p=0.24, two-tailed bootstrap, α = 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about spatial clustering of EX cells.

claim: Individual CO cells and EX cells responded on a sparse subset of trials, and CO and EX cells were heterogeneously distributed within CA1 with little spatial organization.
source: These analyses reveal that individual CO cells and EX cells responded on a sparse subset of trials, and that CO and EX cells were heterogeneously distributed within CA1 with little spatial organization.
evidence: This is a summary of the spatial and temporal response patterns.

claim: Clusters of co-active neuron pairs in the last training session appeared largely not co-active during the extinction session.
source: Clusters of co-active neuron pairs in the last training session appeared largely not co-active during the extinction session (Figure 4Bi, ii).
evidence: This is a finding about network co-activity supported by Figure 4Bi, ii.

claim: Re-clustering the extinction session matrix revealed new clusters of co-active neuron pairs on extinction trials.
source: However, re-clustering the extinction session matrix revealed new clusters of co-active neuron pairs on extinction trials (Figure 4Biii), consistent with our finding of a new population of cells encoding the tone during extinction learning.
evidence: This is a finding about network co-activity during extinction supported by Figure 4Biii.

claim: There was no significant difference in the number of edges present in the last training session versus extinction session (60.0 ± 19.7% vs. 46.4 ± 19.6% of the total edges, t = 0.98, p=0.36, n = 9 mice, two-tailed paired t-test).
source: We found no significant difference in the number of edges present in the last training session versus extinction session (60.0 ± 19.7% vs. 46.4 ± 19.6% of the total edges from the last training and extinction sessions combined, t = 0.98, p=0.36, n = 9 mice, two-tailed paired t-test, Figure 4Di).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about network edge counts.

claim: The connectivity density and degree of the last training and extinction session maps were not different from one another (t = 1.78, p=0.11 and t = 1.82, p=0.11 for density and degree, respectively, n = 9 mice, two-tailed paired t-test).
source: Additionally, the connectivity density (the observed number of edges divided by the total number of possible edges formed between neurons) and degree (two times the average number of edges per neuron) of the two maps were not different from one another (t = 1.78, p=0.11 and t = 1.82, p=0.11 for density and degree, respectively, n = 9 mice, two-tailed paired t-test, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical finding about network properties.

claim: Edges during the last training session appeared largely distinct from edges present during the extinction session.
source: However, when we overlaid the last session and extinction session maps, we noticed that edges during the last training session appeared largely distinct from edges present during the extinction session (Figure 4C, Di).
evidence: This is a finding about network edge identity supported by Figure 4C, Di.

claim: The Jaccard index of common edges between the network maps for the last training and extinction sessions was 8.2%.
source: We found a Jaccard index of 8.2% common edges between the network maps for the last training and extinction sessions, significantly smaller than the 10.4% common edges between the networks for the two trial blocks of the late training session (600 shared edges of 7306 total edges in last training/extinction sessions vs. 2159 shared edges of 20676 total edges in late training session, p=2.48e-08, n = 9 mice, Fisher's exact test, Figure 4C, Dii, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about network edge overlap between conditioning and extinction.

claim: The Jaccard index of common edges between the last training and extinction sessions (8.2%) was significantly smaller than the 10.4% common edges between the networks for the two trial blocks of the late training session (p=2.48e-08, n = 9 mice, Fisher's exact test).
source: We found a Jaccard index of 8.2% common edges between the network maps for the last training and extinction sessions, significantly smaller than the 10.4% common edges between the networks for the two trial blocks of the late training session (600 shared edges of 7306 total edges in last training/extinction sessions vs. 2159 shared edges of 20676 total edges in late training session, p=2.48e-08, n = 9 mice, Fisher's exact test, Figure 4C, Dii, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a statistical finding showing distinct network patterns between conditioning and extinction.

claim: The significant decrease in common edge Jaccard index for the last training and extinction sessions in comparison to that of the two trial blocks of the late training session is consistent with the observation of distinct responsive cells during extinction learning.
source: However, the significant decrease in common edge Jaccard index for the last training and extinction sessions in comparison to that of the two trial blocks of the late training session is consistent with the observation of distinct responsive cells during extinction learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting network and cellular findings.

claim: The distinct activation of different cell pairs suggests unique network patterns of activity during each learning condition, while the overall involvement of the CA1 network (connectivity density) remained constant during the conditioning and extinction training sessions.
source: Furthermore, the distinct activation of different cell pairs suggests unique network patterns of activity during each learning condition, while the overall involvement of the CA1 network (connectivity density) remained constant during the conditioning and extinction training sessions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion about network organization.

claim: This study provides the first detailed, real-time evidence that largely distinct populations of neurons within the hippocampal CA1 region respond to a trace conditioned stimulus during either conditioned learning or extinction learning.
source: In this study, we provide the first detailed, real-time evidence that largely distinct populations of neurons within the hippocampal CA1 region respond to a trace conditioned stimulus during either conditioned learning or extinction learning.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's main contribution.

claim: Previous studies have looked at calcium activity associated with trace conditioning acquisition, but have not investigated whether a separate population of neurons contributes to extinction learning.
source: Previous studies have looked at calcium activity associated with trace conditioning acquisition, but have not investigated whether a separate population of neurons contributes to extinction learning (Zhang et al., 2019; Mohammed et al., 2016; Modi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior work, supported by citations.

claim: Two functionally distinct neuron populations are activated by fear conditioning and extinction in the amygdala.
source: It has been previously reported that two functionally distinct neuron populations are activated by fear conditioning and extinction in the amygdala (Herry et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Herry et al., 2008.

claim: A study looking at the CA1 region of the hippocampus revealed distinct changes in gene phosphorylation states in largely non-overlapping neural populations in either fear conditioning or extinction.
source: Additionally, a subsequent study looking at the CA1 region of the hippocampus revealed distinct changes in gene phosphorylation states in largely non-overlapping neural populations in either fear conditioning or extinction (Tronson et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tronson et al., 2009.

claim: In the Tronson et al. study, cFos and pERK immuno-activities were used as markers of conditioning and extinction learning and measured hours to days after the respective training.
source: However, in this study, cFos and pERK immuno-activities were used as markers of conditioning and extinction learning and measured hours to days after the respective training.
evidence: This describes the methods of the Tronson et al. study.

claim: A synaptic tagging study found populations of cells in the dentate gyrus that are re-activated during either fear conditioning recall or extinction retrieval, presumably representing separate populations.
source: A more recent synaptic tagging study found populations of cells in the dentate gyrus that are re-activated during either fear conditioning recall or extinction retrieval, presumably representing separate populations (Lacagnina et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lacagnina et al., 2019.

claim: In the Lacagnina et al. study, populations were identified using the immediate early gene Arc in separate cohorts of mice, which does not allow for real-time monitoring or direct comparisons between the populations.
source: However, these populations were identified using the immediate early gene Arc in separate cohorts of mice, which does not allow for real-time monitoring or direct comparisons between the populations.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the Lacagnina et al. study.

claim: Trace conditioning lends the advantage of a singular defined stimulus to which neural activity can be easily aligned and measured between the two different paradigms.
source: We applied trace conditioning because (1) it lends the advantage of a singular defined stimulus to which neural activity can be easily aligned and measured between the two different paradigms,
evidence: This is a reasoning statement explaining the choice of trace conditioning.

claim: Trace conditioning allows imaging of the same neurons during both conditioning and extinction in the same imaging session.
source: (2) it allows imaging of the same neurons during both conditioning and extinction in the same imaging session,
evidence: This is a reasoning statement explaining the choice of trace conditioning.

claim: Learning during trace conditioning evolves over multiple trials, unlike fear-based paradigms where learning often occurs over very few trials.
source: and (3) learning during trace conditioning evolves over multiple trials, unlike fear-based paradigms where learning often occurs over very few trials.
evidence: This is a reasoning statement explaining the choice of trace conditioning.

claim: The rate of conditioning was highly animal-dependent, evolving gradually in most animals, but rapidly in a small subset of mice that showed substantial responding to the CS within 40 conditioning trials.
source: Interestingly, we found that the rate of conditioning was highly animal-dependent, evolving gradually in most animals, but rapidly in a small subset of mice that showed substantial responding to the CS within 40 conditioning trials.
evidence: This is a finding about behavioral variability across animals.

claim: Acquisition of trace eye-blink conditioning can occur over dozens of trials in a single session.
source: Although acquisition of trace eye-blink conditioning can occur over dozens of trials in a single session (Modi et al., 2014), most of our animals showed gradual behavioral improvement, reflected in the increase in conditioned response rate after multiple days of training and the increase in the proportion of neurons that responded to the tone from the first to the last training session.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Modi et al., 2014.

claim: The results support the idea that robust conditioned learning gradually evolves over days as CA1 neurons are recruited to encode the stimulus.
source: Overall, our results support the idea that robust conditioned learning gradually evolves over days as CA1 neurons are recruited to encode the stimulus and reflect previous electrophysiology studies in rabbits and rats where the time course of learning evolves through many CS-US pairings (Berger et al., 1983; Green and Arenos, 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data, consistent with prior work.

claim: Extinction learning evolved rapidly, and a new population of neurons that responded to the now-extinguished tone emerged within just 20 extinction trials.
source: In our study, extinction learning evolved rapidly, and a new population of neurons that responded to the now-extinguished tone emerged within just 20 extinction trials.
evidence: This is a summary of the extinction learning findings.

claim: Previous work has implicated the prefrontal cortex and septal cholinergic inputs to be critical to the process of extinction.
source: Previous work has implicated the prefrontal cortex and septal cholinergic inputs to be critical to the process of extinction, and these pathways may play a pivotal role in the rapidity of extinction neuron emergence (Acquas et al., 1996; Chang et al., 2010; Euston et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Acquas et al., 1996; Chang et al., 2010; Euston et al., 2012.

claim: It is possible that extinction learning may occur more rapidly because meaningful associations between conditioning cues and outcomes are already established.
source: In addition, it is possible that extinction learning may occur more rapidly because meaningful associations between conditioning cues and outcomes are already established.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the mechanism of rapid extinction learning.

claim: Studies probing location encoding of familiar places suggest that re-encoding of spatial memory occurs more rapidly when a spatial map is already established and the new information is updating that context.
source: Studies probing location encoding of familiar places, where a spatial memory schema already exists, suggest that re-encoding of spatial memory occurs more rapidly when a spatial map is already established and the new information is updating that context (Tse et al., 2007; McKenzie et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tse et al., 2007 and McKenzie et al., 2013.

claim: The observation of rapid emergence of extinction learning could be due to the presence of a contextual representation of the task stimuli prior to extinction training.
source: Accordingly, our observation of rapid emergence of extinction learning could be due to the presence of a contextual representation of the task stimuli prior to extinction training.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the rapid extinction learning.

claim: Pairwise correlation measured over the brief tone-puff window (600 ms, 12 data points) is unreliable on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: For example, pairwise correlation measured over our brief tone-puff window (600 ms, 12 data points) is unreliable on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of traditional correlation analysis for this dataset.

claim: Co-occurrence-based network approach provides a robust way to observe the trial-by-trial evolution of the population responses.
source: Thus, our development of a co-occurrence-based network approach provides a robust way to observe the trial-by-trial evolution of the population responses and a means to assess contributions of certain cells that might be otherwise overlooked, or overstated, in trial-averaged data.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the co-occurrence analysis method.

claim: CA1 neurons' connectivity patterns change drastically between conditioned trial performance and extinction learning.
source: Using co-occurrence matrices, we found that CA1 neurons' connectivity patterns change drastically between conditioned trial performance and extinction learning.
evidence: This is a summary of the network connectivity findings.

claim: Some cells may participate in both learning conditions.
source: While some cells may participate in both learning conditions, unique pairs of neurons are differentially activated during the different types of learning, indicating a role of network activation in CA1.
evidence: This is a finding about cell participation across learning conditions.

claim: Unique pairs of neurons are differentially activated during the different types of learning, indicating a role of network activation in CA1.
source: While some cells may participate in both learning conditions, unique pairs of neurons are differentially activated during the different types of learning, indicating a role of network activation in CA1.
evidence: This is a conclusion about network-level encoding.

claim: The network connectivity density and degree remain constant across these different behavioral paradigms.
source: However, the network connectivity density and degree remain constant across these different behavioral paradigms, highlighting the constant overall involvement of the CA1 network during both learning tasks.
evidence: This is a summary of the network property findings.

claim: A total of nine female C57BL/6 mice, 8–12 weeks old at the start of the experiments, were used in these studies.
source: A total of nine female C57BL/6 mice, 8–12 weeks old at the start of the experiments, were used in these studies (Taconic; Hudson, NY).
evidence: This describes the animal subjects used in the study.

claim: Power analysis was based on effect size differences found in previous trace conditioning calcium results recorded in the hippocampus.
source: To estimate sample size, power analysis was based on effect size differences found in our previous trace conditioning calcium results recorded in the hippocampus (Mohammed et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the rationale for sample size determination.

claim: Power analysis yielded a sample size of 9.
source: Power analysis was performed using G*Power 3.1.9.6 (http://www.gpower.hhu.de), applying a one-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank test utilizing α = 0.05 and a power (1-β) value of 0.80, and yielded a sample size of 9.
evidence: This describes the result of the power analysis.

claim: Mice were injected with 250 nL of AAV9-Synapsin-GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 virus obtained from the University of Pennsylvania Vector Core (titer ~6e12 GC/mL).
source: Mice were injected with 250 nL of AAV9-Synapsin-GCaMP6f.WPRE.SV40 virus obtained from the University of Pennsylvania Vector Core (titer ~6e12 GC/mL).
evidence: This describes the viral injection procedure.

claim: Animals first underwent viral injection surgery targeting the hippocampus under stereotaxic conditions (AP: −2.0 mm, ML: +1.5 mm, DV: −1.6 mm).
source: Animals first underwent viral injection surgery targeting the hippocampus under stereotaxic conditions (AP: −2.0 mm, ML: +1.5 mm, DV: −1.6 mm).
evidence: This describes the surgical coordinates for viral injection.

claim: Upon complete recovery (7+ days after virus injection), mice underwent a second procedure for the implantation of a sterilized custom imaging cannula.
source: Upon complete recovery (7+ days after virus injection), mice underwent a second procedure for the implantation of a sterilized custom imaging cannula (OD: 3.17 mm, ID: 2.36 mm, height, 2 mm diameter), fitted with a circular coverslip (size 0; OD: 3 mm) adhered using a UV-curable optical adhesive (Norland Products).
evidence: This describes the window implantation procedure.

claim: To access dorsal CA1, the cortical tissue overlying the hippocampus was carefully aspirated away to expose the corpus callosum.
source: To access dorsal CA1, the cortical tissue overlying the hippocampus was carefully aspirated away to expose the corpus callosum.
evidence: This describes the surgical procedure for accessing CA1.

claim: Animals were allowed at least 2 weeks to recover from window surgeries, followed by an additional 2–4 weeks of handling and habituation to being head-fixed underneath the microscope.
source: Animals were allowed at least 2 weeks to recover from window surgeries, followed by an additional 2–4 weeks of handling and habituation to being head-fixed underneath the microscope (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the recovery and habituation period.

claim: Each animal received at least three habituation sessions prior to the first imaging day.
source: Each animal received at least three habituation sessions prior to the first imaging day.
evidence: This describes the habituation protocol.

claim: Inter-trial intervals for each presentation were pseudo-randomized within a recording session with an inter-trial interval of 35 ± 5 s.
source: Inter-trial intervals for each presentation were pseudo-randomized within a recording session with an inter-trial interval of 35 ± 5 s.
evidence: This describes the timing of trial presentations.

claim: Animals were first presented with 20 tone-only trials.
source: Animals were first presented with 20 tone-only trials.
evidence: This describes the initial training protocol.

claim: Animals were then presented with either 60 tone-puff trials per day for 8 days or 80 tone-puff trials per day for 4 days.
source: Animals were then presented with either 60 tone-puff trials per day for 8 days or 80 tone-puff trials per day for 4 days.
evidence: This describes the conditioning training protocol.

claim: The final recording session consisted of 20 or 40 tone-puff conditioning trials, followed by 40 extinction trials, where the puff was removed but the tone remained.
source: The final recording session consisted of 20 or 40 tone-puff conditioning trials, followed by 40 extinction trials, where the puff was removed but the tone remained.
evidence: This describes the final session protocol.

claim: Images yielded a field of view 1.343 mm by 1.343 mm (1024 × 1024 pixels) and were acquired at a 20 Hz sampling rate.
source: Images yielded a field of view 1.343 mm by 1.343 mm (1024 × 1024 pixels) and were acquired at a 20 Hz sampling rate and stored offline for analysis.
evidence: This describes the imaging parameters.

claim: A conditioned response was classified by a threshold of 2% eye area deviation below the standard eye area.
source: A conditioned response was classified by a threshold of 2% eye area deviation below the standard eye area.
evidence: This describes the criterion for identifying conditioned responses.

claim: Eye traces for six mice were manually inspected by an independent observer to confirm that eyelid movements ('blinks') identified using the 2% threshold matched blinks selected by visual inspection.
source: Eye traces for six mice were manually inspected by an independent observer to confirm that eyelid movements ('blinks') identified using the 2% threshold matched blinks selected by visual inspection.
evidence: This describes the validation of the automated blink detection method.

claim: The final 20 CS-US trials of the first imaging day were chosen for analysis to avoid potential startle response to novel stimuli (especially the puff) in the mice.
source: As stated previously, the final 20 CS-US trials of the first imaging day were chosen for analysis. These trials were chosen to avoid potential startle response to novel stimuli (especially the puff) in the mice, and because calcium response latency was shorter during these trials as compared to the first 20 CS-US trials of the first imaging day.
evidence: This explains the rationale for trial selection.

claim: Average response latency in the first 20 trials of the first imaging day was 470.3 ± 214.1 ms, and by the last 20 trials of the same imaging day, average latency dropped to 436.9 ± 202.9 ms.
source: Latency of calcium response was determined as the average onset time of the first calcium event after tone onset across trials for each responsive cell. Average response latency in the first 20 trials of the first imaging day was 470.3 ± 214.1 ms, and by the last 20 trials of the same imaging day, average latency dropped to 436.9 ± 202.9 ms (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), suggesting a reduction in response to the eye puff after the first 20 trials of the first imaging day.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about response latency changes within the first session.

claim: Shorter response latency is consistent with the idea that the neuronal response is shifting from being puff-responsive to being tone-responsive.
source: Shorter response latency is consistent with the idea that the neuronal response is shifting from being puff-responsive to being tone-responsive.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the latency data.

claim: Motion correction of videos was done using ptmc, an open-source, parallel Python version of an image stabilization process published previously.
source: Motion correction of videos was done using ptmc, an open-source, parallel Python version (github.com/HanLabBU/ptmc) of an image stabilization process published previously (Mohammed et al., 2016; Hansen, 2017a).
evidence: This describes the motion correction method.

claim: After motion correction, regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to cells were selected using a semi-automated custom MATLAB software called SemiSeg.
source: After motion correction, regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to cells were selected using a semi-automated custom MATLAB software called SemiSeg (github.com/HanLabBU/SemiSeg) (Hansen, 2017b).
evidence: This describes the cell segmentation method.

claim: The baseline calcium level was calculated for each cell by fitting a normal distribution to the lowest 50 percentile of the data and using the mean of this distribution as the baseline calcium level.
source: Therefore, the baseline calcium level was calculated for each cell by fitting a normal distribution to the lowest 50 percentile of the data (assuming a Gaussian noise fluctuation surrounding a true baseline calcium level) and using the mean of this distribution as the baseline calcium level (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes the normalization method for calcium traces.

claim: Onsets of calcium events can be detected using Fourier analysis, where event onset coincides with increasing low-frequency power.
source: Onsets of calcium events can be detected using Fourier analysis, where event onset coincides with increasing low-frequency power.
evidence: This describes the calcium event detection method.

claim: Any identified calcium event with amplitude less than seven standard deviations of the trace in the 10 s time window prior to calcium event onset was excluded.
source: Any identified calcium event with amplitude (the signal difference between the peak and the event onset) less than seven standard deviations of the trace in the 10 s time window prior to calcium event onset was excluded.
evidence: This describes the threshold for calcium event detection.

claim: 1 s was chosen as the response window to allow for the slow kinetics of calcium signaling.
source: 1 s was chosen as the response window to allow for the slow kinetics of calcium signaling (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the response window duration.

claim: Spectral biclustering is an unsupervised clustering method initially developed for clustering microarray gene expression data.
source: Spectral biclustering is an unsupervised clustering method initially developed for clustering microarray gene expression data (Kluger et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the spectral biclustering method.
